Interdisciplinary cooperation within organoid technologies has the potential to contribute to the treatment of various diseases. The publication of organoid research papers has undergone exponential growth since 2015, accounting for over 72% of the total, thereby underscoring the field’s expansion. The significance of organoids in cancer, drug screening, and regenerative medicine is highlighted, reflecting the field’s impact on medicine. Organoid technology achieved key breakthroughs in the early 21st century. Clevers’ team constructed the first miniature intestinal organoid [ ] in 2009, and Knoblich’s team developed brain organoids [ ] in 2013, further advancing the technology’s application in simulating complex organ development and disease research. With subsequent research progress, organoid technology has continued to mature, and related literature has increased year by year. Several bibliometric studies have examined the research landscape of organoids. However, their analytical scope remains markedly limited. First, many existing bibliometric studies provide only broad-level productivity counts without dissecting the structure, evolution, and impact of international and institutional collaborative networks that drive the field. Second, previous analyses often remain within the realm of academic literature, failing to integrate data from the patent domain to trace the critical pathway from scientific discovery to technological application and potential clinical translation. Third, there is a paucity of studies that systematically map how insights and methodologies from distinct disciplines (e.g., stem cell biology, bioengineering, materials science, and computational analysis) converge to advance organoid research. To address these shortcomings, this study utilizes bibliometrics and visualization techniques to analyze organoid research publications from the last two decades, thereby revealing trends, identifying key influencers, exploring collaboration networks, and pinpointing research hotspots and emerging themes. First, our work uniquely associates global collaboration structures with citation impact, enabling a rigorous comparison of the scientific influence of major collaborative axis (e.g., United States–Europe vs United States–Asia). Furthermore, by integrating bibliometric, patent analysis, and clinical-translation evidence, this study firstly constructs a full organoid translational development chain that links basic research, technological innovation, and emerging clinical applications. Importantly, this study also underscores the interdisciplinary fusion that anchors the field’s advancement, offering insights into how cross-domain interactions collectively drive the evolution of organoid technologies. Collectively, these innovations enable this study to offer a more comprehensive and translationally informed mapping of the organoid field than previously available, providing perspectives that extend beyond those presented in earlier bibliometric studies. As an important scientific research tool, organoid technology mimics the functions and properties of real organs by using three-dimensional structures derived from human stem cells. This provides valuable resources for various fields, including medical research, new drug development, regenerative medicine, and personalized therapy. In the future, the impact of organoid technology is expected to increase even further, playing a crucial role in advancing human health and medical technology. Cancer organoid models This cluster primarily focuses on the cancer organoid models, with core keywords including “cancer (1064),” “organoid culture (105),” “glioblastoma (103),” “patient-derived organoids (165),” “heterogeneity (191),” “tumor (370),” “biobank (121),” and their implications for “drug screening (155),” and therapeutic evaluation. The foundation of organoid technology was laid by advancements in stem cell biology throughout the 20th century. While the term “organoid” was formally proposed earlier, a pivotal milestone was reached in 2009 when Hans Clevers and his team successfully cultivated miniature intestinal organoids [ ] derived from a single Lgr5 + adult stem cell in mice for the first time. This breakthrough demonstrated the remarkable self-organization potential of stem cells [ ] . Combined with the standardized culture substrate known as “matrigel,” it formed the core methodology of modern organoid technology, marking the beginning of its foundational period. Shortly thereafter, Knoblich’s team [ ] published a groundbreaking paper in Nature, establishing the first method for cultivating three-dimensional brain organoids from human pluripotent stem cells. This advancement expanded the application scope of organoids in simulating complex organ development and disease research, laying the experimental foundation for the formation of related research clusters. As core methodologies matured, organoid technology entered an application and expansion phase, most notably driven by its adoption in cancer research. Applying organoid technology to cancer models represents one of the most promising areas in contemporary biomedical research, significantly advancing personalized medicine and cancer biology studies. With the development of organoid culture technology, researchers have successfully cultured many cancer organoids, including rectal [ ] , gastric [ , ] , pancreatic [ , ] , breast [ , ] , and glioblastoma [ , ] . By using tumor cells from specific patients to culture organoids, researchers can study individual differences in cancer in greater detail, offering new perspectives for preclinical models of human diseases and personalized treatment strategies. Critically, cancer organoids offer distinct advantages over traditional preclinical models. Unlike conventional 2D cell lines, PDOs retain the spatial architecture, cellular heterogeneity, and genetic landscape of the original tumor. Compared to patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models in mice, organoids can be established more efficiently and at a lower cost, allowing for more scalable and high-throughput drug screening and functional genomics. A key breakthrough was the creation of large-scale living organoid biobanks [ , – ] around 2015, directly addressing the bottlenecks in scale and quantity faced by traditional models. These biobanks, which encompass both healthy and tumor tissues, capture the genetic and phenotypic diversity of patient populations, enabling systematic studies of tumor biology and drug response across a multitude of genomic backgrounds. By culturing organoids from individual patients, researchers can delve into the molecular basis of tumor heterogeneity. This advances drug screening from basic research toward preclinical drug sensitivity testing and personalized therapeutic strategies, significantly bridging the gap between fundamental cancer biology and clinical application. We are currently in an era of increasing model complexity and precision, driven by cross-disciplinary integration with a range of emerging technologies. Researchers are integrating organoids with microfluidic organ-on-a-chip platforms [ ] , CRISPR gene editing [ ] , and single-cell sequencing technologies [ ] . This convergence is propelling organoid models toward highly biomimetic miniature organs, significantly expanding their application boundaries in disease modeling and drug discovery. Drugs that can be screened using organoids include chemotherapeutic drugs, small-molecule targeted drugs, and antibody drugs. Organoids can be combined with a variety of technologies to improve their functionality and range of applications. The combination of organoids and bioprinting technology allows for the precise control of organoid architecture and the creation of tissues with mechanical properties specific to the microenvironment [ ] . The combination of organoids and microfluidics [ ] provides precise control of the organoid culture environment, including pH, oxygen, and nutrient supply, and waste removal. This technology also facilitates the engineering of vascularized organoids by guiding fluid dynamics to mimic the curvature and branching of natural blood vessels, thereby improving physiological relevance and supporting the study of vascular-related diseases. Choi et al [ ] demonstrated the utility of microfluidic cancer organoids by using patient-derived microfluidic cancer organoids from pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma to test several chemotherapeutic treatments, including glycogen synthase kinase inhibitors. Organ chips simulate near-physiological tissue microenvironments by integrating the advantages of organ-like and microchip technologies [ ] , guiding stem cell behaviors and organ-like morphogenesis, and constructing multiorgan chips or even human body chips represents a long-term goal of this field. As disease models, organoids enable researchers to elucidate disease activation mechanisms at the molecular and cellular levels, helping to study disease intervention and treatment better. For example, signaling pathways such as the WNT/β-catenin and MAPK pathway [ ] , which are frequently dysregulated in cancer, can be directly interrogated using organoid models to validate the dynamic interactions within and between core signaling pathways in maintaining tumor growth and initiating malignant processes. These models reveal how complex molecular networks drive tumorigenesis through kinase activation, phosphorylation events, and changes in receptor-ligand binding. They also facilitate investigations into DNA damage response, epigenetic modifications (e.g., methylation patterns), and the emergence of senescent or resistant phenotypes, informing the development of therapeutic strategies. Furthermore, their capacity for large-scale expansion under controlled culture conditions makes them highly suitable for clinical applications. Multiple studies [ , ] have confirmed the broad potential of organoid regeneration strategies for treating various diseases. The intestinal organoid model has a mature system and was first used in regenerative medicine. Avansino et al [ ] transplanted murine small intestinal adult stem cell-derived organoids were transplanted into the jejunum of recipient mice, demonstrating that the organoids were able to grow new small intestinal mucosa in the transplanted area and differentiate into intestinal epithelial cells and goblet cells. In the highly regarded field of liver regeneration, patient-specific liver organoids hold promise for overcoming critical bottlenecks of donor shortage and immune rejection. Current liver transplantation faces immune-related challenges, while scalable production of human liver organoids offers a potential solution. Hu et al [ ] transplanted human fetal liver-like organs into a mouse model of liver injury, and the results demonstrated that liver-like organs can significantly expand and regenerate damaged liver tissue after transplantation. The integration of organoids with gene editing and bioengineering technologies further expands their therapeutic potential. Clevers et al [ ] used CRISPR-dependent single-base editing to repair mutations in the CFTR causative gene in cystic fibrosis patient samples from the Dutch Organoid Biobank, providing a clinically matched therapeutic option for cystic fibrosis disease. Wu et al [ ] established a multifunctional blastocyst complementation platform based on CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genome editing of fertilized eggs. The rat pancreas was grown in vivo in mice. The rat pancreas was grown in vivo in mice, successfully demonstrating interspecies blastocyst complementation in pancreas-knockout mice. Looking forward, personalized stem cell-derived organoids may help overcome the immune rejection of artificial organ transplants, and the deep integration of micro- and nanoengineering–based organ maturation and personalized organoid transplantation is expected to advance regenerative organ therapies. Nanotechnology-constructed biomaterial scaffolds provide an environment conducive to cell adhesion, differentiation, and proliferation for the self-organization of organoid pluripotent stem cells [ ] . In addition, microfluidic technology controls the differentiation of stem cells to repair nervous system damage, providing new opportunities for regenerative medicine. Together, these converging technologies are paving the way for organoid-based regenerative therapies. Current challenges and remaining limitations in organoid research However, alongside these remarkable advances, the field confronts significant challenges and limitations that must be addressed to fully realize its translational potential. A primary biological constraint is the frequent absence of key microenvironmental components, such as functional vasculature and immune cells, which restricts nutrient diffusion, limits long-term culture, and hampers the modeling of systemic interactions. Technically, the reliance on ill-defined matrices like Matrigel and a lack of standardized protocols impede reproducibility and scalability, posing barriers to clinical adoption. In oncology, patient-derived tumor organoids may fail to capture the full heterogeneity of the original malignancy, potentially biasing drug-response predictions. Furthermore, the rapid progression of brain organoids has sparked ethical debates concerning the emergence of neural complexity and consciousness. Addressing these limitations – through engineered vascularization, immune integration, defined culture systems, and ethical frameworks – is crucial for transforming organoids from a powerful research model into a robust platform for personalized medicine and regenerative therapies. Limitations As with other bibliometric studies, this paper has several limitations. Only English-language publications were selected, and there may be a language bias. Furthermore, there are differences in authors’ and institutions’ attributions, which may cause bias in the statistical results. Finally, given the timing of the retrieval, the 2024 data remain incomplete. Conclusion Organoid-related research witnessed a period of exponential growth between 2000 and 2024, a phenomenon indicative of the enduring interest of scholars and the transformative potential of this research area. The United States, with institutions such as Harvard University at the forefront, is the foremost contributor in terms of both output and impact. The field is propelled forward by influential journals such as Cell and leading authors such as Hans Clevers. Notable research areas include cancer organoid models, drug screening, innovative technical and molecular mechanisms, and regenerative medicine. This study emphasizes the advancements and global collaborations in organoids, underscoring their role as a catalyst for biomedical research. Organoids are considered as a pivotal tool for enhancing the comprehension of complex diseases, thereby providing unparalleled avenues for scientific discovery.

Interprofessional education for collaborative practice (IPECP) in prelicensure education promotes professional/interprofessional socialization. Within IPECP, students gain understanding of their professional role and begin developing an interprofessional identity, including collaborative skills, attitudes, and behaviours. IPECP literature in oral health education is limited. It is not well understood how oral health students are involved in IPECP and prepared for collaborative practice. Objective: To assess the literature on IPECP within oral health education and identify IPECP models and characteristics of experiences enabling professional/interprofessional socialization, interprofessional identity development, and readiness for collaborative practice. Methods: Guided by JBI methodology, the research team searched CINAHL, DOSS, MEDLINE, and APAPsycInfo for peer-reviewed articles on IPECP models in prelicensure education of oral health students. Articles (N = 321) were screened by 2 reviewers for title/abstract, followed by full text. Twenty-eight articles were included. Results: Single and multiformat IPECP models were identified including workshops, case studies, simulation, and clinical experiences. Characteristics of IPECP experiences were identified and categorized as: 1) learning from and about others; 2) establishing social connections; 3) authenticity of experiences; and 4) consistent socialization and exposure. However, challenges for IPECP in oral health education persist, including siloed education and a lack of intentional IPECP curriculum. Conclusion: Increased integration of oral health students into health professions IPECP and consistent exposure throughout programs is needed. IPECP curriculum must enable all students to explore their professional contributions to interprofessional teams. IPECP for developing an interprofessional identity in oral health students remains understudied; longitudinal and qualitative analyses are needed. Contexte : La collaboration interprofessionnelle favorise l’amélioration des soins et des résultats pour les patients. La Interprofessional Education and Collaborative Practice (formation interprofessionnelle et pratique collaborative, ou IPECP) dans l’éducation préalable à l’agrément favorise la socialisation professionnelle/interprofessionnelle. Au sein de l’IPECP, les étudiants acquièrent une compréhension de leur rôle professionnel et commencent à développer une identité interprofessionnelle, y compris des compétences, des attitudes et des comportements collaboratifs. La documentation de l’IPECP sur la formation en santé buccodentaire est limitée. On ne comprend pas bien comment les étudiants en santé buccodentaire participent à l’IPECP et y sont préparés à la pratique collaborative. Objectif : Évaluer la documentation sur l’IPECP dans le cadre de la formation en santé buccodentaire et déterminer les modèles et les caractéristiques des expériences qui permettent la socialisation professionnelle et interprofessionnelle, le développement de l’identité interprofessionnelle et l’état de préparation à la pratique collaborative. Méthodes : Guidée par la méthodologie JBI, l’équipe de recherche a effectué des recherches dans CINAHL, DOSS, MEDLINE et APAPsycInfo pour trouver des articles évalués par les pairs sur les modèles IPECP dans l’éducation préalable à l’agrément des étudiants en santé buccodentaire. Les articles (N = 321) ont été examinés par 2 examinateurs pour le titre/résumé, suivis du texte intégral. Vingt-huit articles ont été inclus. Résultats : Des modèles IPECP mono et multiformat ont été identifiés, y compris des ateliers, des études de cas, des simulations et des expériences cliniques. Les caractéristiques des expériences de l’IPECP ont été déterminées et classées comme suit : 1) apprentissage des autres et à leur sujet; 2) établissement des liens sociaux; 3) authenticité des expériences; 4) socialisation et exposition cohérentes. Toutefois, les défis liés à l’IPECP en matière de formation en santé buccodentaire persistent, y compris l’éducation cloisonnée et l’absence d’un programme intentionnel de l’IPECP. Conclusion : Une intégration accrue des étudiants en santé buccodentaire aux professions de la santé par l’entremise de l’IPECP et une exposition uniforme dans l’ensemble des programmes sont nécessaires. Le programme d’études de l’IPECP doit permettre à tous les étudiants d’explorer leurs contributions professionnelles aux équipes interprofessionnelles.
